title: How do you design a reliable benchmark for a JVM service? Explain the warmup phase and JIT compilation from C1 to C2, accounting for GC cycles, using HdrHistogram, isolating the bottleneck, and initialising the connection pool before measuring.
shortTitle: How to design a JVM benchmark?
keyPoints: HotSpot interprets bytecode, then C1 compiles with profiling, then C2 heavily optimises hot methods.
Warmup must drive the hot path to C2 with realistic data mix before measuring.
Dead-code elimination can delete unused benchmark results; consume results via a blackhole or field.
GC must reach steady state; run long enough for several cycles and fix heap size with -Xms equal to -Xmx.
HdrHistogram records every latency losslessly; never report only averages.
Pre-initialise connection pools, caches, and TLS sessions before the measurement window.
JMH handles warmup, forking, and blackholes via annotations for micro-benchmarks.

s1_definition.oneliner: A trustworthy JVM benchmark warms up until C2 has compiled the hot path and GC is steady, pre-initialises pools and caches, records every latency into HdrHistogram, and isolates the one component under test.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Warmup phase** – drive the hot methods through C1 and into C2 compilation before recording any measurements.
- **GC steady state** – run long enough for garbage collection to settle; fix heap size with `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx`.
- **HdrHistogram** – record every latency value into logarithmically sized buckets for accurate high percentiles.
- **Isolation** – pre-initialise connection pools, caches, and TLS sessions so cold-start costs do not pollute the histogram.
- **JMH** – Java Microbenchmark Harness: handles warmup, forking, and dead-code prevention via annotations.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine timing how fast a new teller at National Bank of India serves customers. On the first morning the teller is slow, reading the manual for every step (interpreting). After a few dozen customers they remember the common steps (C1). After a few hundred they are an expert on autopilot (C2). A good benchmark lets the teller become expert first (warmup), makes sure the cash drawer is already stocked (pool initialised), ignores the one coffee break (does not confuse a GC pause with normal work), and writes down every single service time (HdrHistogram) instead of just the average.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  JVM Compilation Tiers:
  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐
  │Interpreter│──▶│   C1     │──▶│   C2     │
  │  (slow)   │    │ (fast-ish)│   │ (fast)   │
  │           │    │+profiling │   │+inlining │
  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘
       ▲               ▲               ▲
  First calls    ~100 calls       ~10K calls
  DO NOT         Still warming    NOW MEASURE
  MEASURE        up                HERE

  Benchmark Timeline:
  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐
  │  Warmup    │  │ GC Settle  │  │ Measurement│
  │  C1 → C2  │  │ Steady heap│  │ HdrHistogram│
  │  Pool init │  │ Fix -Xms/mx│  │ p50,p99,p999│
  └────────────┘  └────────────┘  └────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A reliable JVM benchmark respects how HotSpot actually runs code. It starts by interpreting, then C1 compiles with profiling, and finally C2 produces heavily optimised code. Measuring before C2 benchmarks the interpreter, not the production hot path.

I always run an explicit warmup with realistic data, fix the heap size, pre-initialise pools and caches, and record every latency into HdrHistogram. JMH handles all of this for micro-benchmarks through annotations.

At National Bank of India this discipline turned our benchmarks from misleading cold-JVM numbers into stable, trustworthy percentiles that we gate every release against.

Remember one sentence: warm up until C2 compiles the hot path, fix the heap, pre-initialise pools, record every latency into HdrHistogram, and never report only averages.
